gloss: The place where a person does their job.
examples: Cell phones aren't allowed in the *workplace*.
The company is trying to make the *workplace* safer.
These rules apply in most American *workplaces*.

gloss: A small work area separated from the rest of an office by low walls.
examples: He spends nine hours a day in a *cubicle*.
Somebody taped a birthday sign to her *cubicle*.
They tore out the *cubicles* and went open-plan.

gloss: The counter near the entrance where visitors check in.
examples: Leave your name at the *front desk*.
The *front desk* called up to say my ride was here.
Both *front desks* were empty at that hour.

gloss: Someone whose job is to greet visitors and answer the phone at an office.
examples: The *receptionist* buzzed us in.
Ask the *receptionist* for a visitor badge.
They hired two more *receptionists* for the clinic.

gloss: A place at a workplace or school where meals are served and eaten.
examples: We had lunch in the company *cafeteria*.
The *cafeteria* closes at two.
Both *cafeterias* serve the same sandwiches.

gloss: A room at work where employees can eat, rest, or make coffee.
examples: There's leftover pizza in the *break room*.
Somebody left a mess in the *break room* again.
The *break rooms* on both floors have microwaves.

gloss: A large building where goods are stored before they are sold or shipped.
examples: Your order is still sitting in the *warehouse*.
He drove a forklift in a *warehouse* for six years.
They're building two new *warehouses* off the highway.

gloss: A building where goods are made in large quantities by machine.
examples: Her dad worked at the *factory* for thirty years.
The *factory* shut down right after the recession.
Most of these parts come from *factories* overseas.

gloss: A local office or store belonging to a larger company.
examples: Our downtown *branch* opens at nine.
She manages the Chicago *branch*.
The bank closed four *branches* last year.

gloss: One of the sections a company or organization is divided into.
examples: She works in the accounting *department*.
That's a question for the legal *department*.
Three *departments* share the same floor.

gloss: A business, especially one providing professional services.
examples: He's a partner at a law *firm*.
The *firm* has offices in four cities.
A lot of small *firms* went under that year.

gloss: A group of people working together for a shared purpose.
examples: She runs a nonprofit *organization*.
The whole *organization* got the same email.
Several *organizations* signed the letter.
contrast: Americans spell it with a z; the British usually write organisation.

gloss: A new company, usually small and trying to grow fast.
examples: He left a big company to join a *startup*.
The *startup* ran out of money in under a year.
Half her friends work at tech *startups*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A particular branch of business, or manufacturing in general.
examples: She's worked in the music *industry* since college.
The airline *industry* took a huge hit that year.
Several *industries* are still short on workers.

gloss: A machine that puts text or images from a computer onto paper.
examples: The *printer* is out of paper again.
Send it to the *printer* on the third floor.
Both *printers* are jammed.

gloss: A machine that makes paper copies of documents.
examples: The *copier* jams every other day.
She stood at the *copier* for twenty minutes.
They finally replaced both *copiers*.
contrast: Also called a photocopier; Americans often just say the copy machine.

gloss: A small bent piece of wire that holds sheets of paper together.
examples: Hand me a *paperclip*.
The whole packet was held together with one *paperclip*.
There's a box of *paperclips* in the drawer.
contrast: Often written as two words: paper clip.

gloss: A stiff folder with rings inside that hold punched pages.
examples: Everything for the class is in this *binder*.
She put the contract in a three-ring *binder*.
The *binders* are on the shelf by the window.

gloss: A folded cover for holding loose papers, or a place for files on a computer.
examples: Put the receipts in a *folder*.
I saved it in a *folder* on my desktop.
There were a dozen *folders* stacked on his chair.

gloss: A set of documents kept together, or a piece of data stored on a computer.
examples: Can you email me the *file*?
Her employee *file* goes back ten years.
He keeps all the tax *files* in the cabinet.

gloss: A smooth white panel you write on with markers that wipe off.
examples: She drew the whole plan on the *whiteboard*.
Somebody erased the *whiteboard* before we finished.
Every conference room has a *whiteboard*.

gloss: A device that shines an image from a computer onto a screen or wall.
examples: The *projector* won't connect to my laptop.
Dim the lights and turn on the *projector*.
Both *projectors* are booked for that hour.

gloss: The screen you look at when using a computer.
examples: He works with two *monitors*.
The *monitor* keeps flickering.
IT ordered a bigger *monitor* for her desk.

gloss: The set of keys you type on to control a computer.
examples: I spilled coffee on my *keyboard*.
This *keyboard* is way too loud.
They ordered new *keyboards* for the whole floor.

gloss: A small portable computer that folds shut.
examples: Bring your *laptop* to the meeting.
My *laptop* died halfway through the call.
The company issues *laptops* to everyone.

gloss: An electronic machine for storing information and doing work with it.
examples: My *computer* is running really slow today.
Turn the *computer* off before you leave.
All the *computers* were updated overnight.

gloss: A book of blank pages for writing notes in.
examples: She takes notes in a little *notebook*.
I left my *notebook* in the conference room.
There's a stack of *notebooks* in the supply closet.

gloss: A writing instrument that uses ink.
examples: Do you have a *pen* I can borrow?
The *pen* ran out halfway through the form.
Somebody keeps walking off with my *pens*.

gloss: A writing instrument with a thin stick of graphite inside.
examples: Fill out the form in pen, not *pencil*.
He sat there chewing on a *pencil*.
These *pencils* all need sharpening.

gloss: A small piece of rubber or felt used to rub out writing.
examples: Is there an *eraser* on that pencil?
She rubbed the line out with an *eraser*.
The *erasers* for the whiteboard have disappeared again.
contrast: American word; the British say rubber for the pencil kind.

gloss: A flat paper cover that a letter goes into for mailing.
examples: He sealed the check in an *envelope*.
Write the address on the *envelope*.
There's a box of *envelopes* by the printer.

gloss: A chart or program showing the days of the year and what is planned on them.
examples: Put it on the *calendar* so I don't forget.
My *calendar* is packed all week.
Our *calendars* never seem to line up.
contrast: Ends in -ar, not -er, even though it sounds like -er.

gloss: Paper, envelopes, and other writing supplies.
examples: The office orders all its *stationery* online.
We're out of *stationery* again.
She keeps the *stationery* in the bottom drawer.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *stationary* ('not moving'); the paper one ends in -ery.

gloss: The everyday materials a workplace uses up, like paper and pens.
examples: We're low on office *supplies*.
The *supplies* are kept in the closet by the copier.
Order more *supplies* before the end of the month.
contrast: Used in the plural for office materials — *a supply* means something else.

gloss: A small square of paper with glue on one edge, used for short reminders.
examples: He left a *sticky note* on my monitor.
The whole report was covered in *sticky notes*.
Write it on a *sticky note* so you remember.

gloss: A written account of work done or facts found out.
examples: The *report* is due Friday morning.
She wrote a twelve-page *report* on the numbers.
Nobody reads these *reports* anyway.

gloss: A talk in which someone shows and explains information to a group.
examples: I'm giving a *presentation* to the whole department.
His *presentation* ran about ten minutes long.
We sat through four *presentations* in a row.

gloss: A computer document laid out in rows and columns for numbers.
examples: Everything's tracked in one big *spreadsheet*.
She sent me the *spreadsheet* with the budget in it.
He keeps three separate *spreadsheets* for expenses.

gloss: A piece of writing that gives official information or a record.
examples: Sign the *document* at the bottom of page two.
I can't open the *document* you sent.
Bring both *documents* to the meeting.

gloss: A legal agreement in writing between two sides.
examples: Read the *contract* before you sign anything.
Her *contract* runs through December.
They lost two big *contracts* this quarter.
contrast: Stress moves: the noun is KAHN-trakt, the verb *to contract* is kuhn-TRAKT.

gloss: An arrangement that two sides have accepted.
examples: We finally reached an *agreement*.
The *agreement* covers the next three years.
Both *agreements* were signed the same day.

gloss: A document listing goods or work and asking for payment.
examples: I sent the *invoice* two weeks ago.
The *invoice* is due in thirty days.
They're still sitting on three unpaid *invoices*.

gloss: A slip of paper proving that something was paid for.
examples: Keep the *receipt* in case you need to return it.
I can't get reimbursed without a *receipt*.
She had a shoebox full of *receipts*.
contrast: The p is silent: rih-SEET.

gloss: A plan for how much money will be spent on something.
examples: That's not in the *budget* this year.
We came in under *budget* for once.
The *budgets* for both projects got cut.

gloss: Money spent on something, especially for work.
examples: The trip was a big *expense*.
Submit your *expenses* by the end of the month.
Meals count as a business *expense*.

gloss: The payment an employee gets for a period of work.
examples: My *paycheck* hits the account every other Friday.
Taxes come straight out of your *paycheck*.
A lot of people here live *paycheck* to *paycheck*.
contrast: American; the British write pay cheque, or say payslip for the document.

gloss: The list of a company's employees and the money paid to them.
examples: There are forty people on the *payroll*.
Talk to *payroll* about the missing hours.
Both *payrolls* are handled by the same office.

gloss: The forms and written records a job requires.
examples: There's a mountain of *paperwork* on his desk.
I spent all morning on *paperwork*.
You can't start until the *paperwork* goes through.
contrast: Uncountable — say *a lot of paperwork*, never *paperworks*.

gloss: A printed sheet with blank spaces to be filled in.
examples: Fill out this *form* and bring it back.
The *form* asks for your Social Security number.
There were four *forms* to sign on my first day.

gloss: A set of questions asked of many people to collect opinions.
examples: HR sent out an employee *survey*.
The *survey* takes about five minutes.
Nobody fills out these *surveys*.
contrast: Stress moves: the noun is SUR-vay, the verb *to survey* is sur-VAY.

gloss: A ready-made pattern you fill in to make a document.
examples: Just use the *template* instead of starting over.
The *template* already has the logo on it.
There are *templates* for all the standard letters.

gloss: Your name written by hand to show you agree to something.
examples: We just need your *signature* here.
The *signature* on the check didn't match.
They collected *signatures* from everyone on the team.
contrast: The g is pronounced here, though it is silent in *sign*.

gloss: A short written summary of your work history, sent when applying for a job.
examples: Send me your *resume* and I'll pass it along.
Her *resume* is two pages long.
They got over two hundred *resumes* for one opening.
contrast: Often written résumé. The noun is REZ-uh-may; the verb *resume* ('start again') is rih-ZOOM.

gloss: A letter sent with a resume explaining why you want the job.
examples: Don't send a resume without a *cover letter*.
Her *cover letter* was better than the resume.
He rewrites the *cover letter* for every job.

gloss: A written plan or offer put forward for others to consider.
examples: We're putting together a *proposal* for the client.
The *proposal* got turned down.
They reviewed six *proposals* before choosing one.

gloss: A rough calculation of what something will cost or how long it will take.
examples: Can you give me an *estimate* by Thursday?
The *estimate* came in way over what we expected.
We got three *estimates* before hiring anyone.
contrast: Stress stays on ES-, but the ending changes: the noun is ES-tuh-muht, the verb ES-tuh-mayt.

gloss: The written record of what was said and decided at a meeting.
examples: Who's taking the *minutes* today?
The *minutes* from last week are attached.
She reads the *minutes* out loud at the start.
contrast: Always plural in this meaning — never *a minute* of a meeting.

gloss: An official rule or approach that an organization follows.
examples: That's against company *policy*.
The new *policy* takes effect in January.
They rewrote all the vacation *policies*.

gloss: An official examination of a company's records or accounts.
examples: The company is going through an *audit*.
The *audit* turned up a few errors.
They survived two *audits* in one year.

gloss: An occasion when people come together to discuss work.
examples: I've got a *meeting* at ten.
That *meeting* could have been an email.
His calendar is nothing but back-to-back *meetings*.

gloss: A large organized event where people meet to hear talks about their field.
examples: She's speaking at a *conference* in Denver.
The *conference* runs Tuesday through Thursday.
He goes to two or three *conferences* a year.

gloss: A conversation by phone or video, especially a work one.
examples: I'm on a *call* until eleven.
Let's set up a *call* for Monday.
She had five *calls* back to back.

gloss: The time by which something has to be finished.
examples: The *deadline* is end of day Friday.
We missed the *deadline* by two hours.
He works better with tight *deadlines*.

gloss: A plan showing when things will happen.
examples: My *schedule* is full this week.
The project is behind *schedule*.
They post the *schedules* every Sunday night.
contrast: Americans say SKEJ-ool; the British say SHED-yool.

gloss: Something you are trying to achieve.
examples: Our *goal* is to double sales this year.
She set a *goal* of finishing by June.
We hit all three *goals* for the quarter.

gloss: The latest news about how something is going.
examples: Can you give me a quick *update*?
There's been no *update* since Tuesday.
He sends *updates* every Friday afternoon.
contrast: Stress moves: the noun is UP-dayt, the verb *to update* is up-DAYT.

gloss: A careful look at how well someone or something is doing.
examples: I have my performance *review* next week.
The *review* went better than I expected.
They do *reviews* twice a year here.

gloss: The series of jobs a person has in one line of work over their life.
examples: She spent her whole *career* in publishing.
That mistake nearly ended his *career*.
A lot of people change *careers* in their thirties.
contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable, kuh-REER — don't confuse it with *carrier*.

gloss: The paid position a person holds.
examples: He got a *job* at a bank downtown.
She's been at the same *job* for eleven years.
He worked two *jobs* to pay for school.
contrast: Countable, unlike *work*: say *two jobs*, never *two works*.

gloss: A particular job within an organization.
examples: I'm applying for a *position* in marketing.
The *position* has been open since March.
They're filling three *positions* this fall.

gloss: The job or function a person has on a team.
examples: She just moved into a management *role*.
My *role* is mostly writing and editing.
The two *roles* overlap quite a bit.

gloss: A kind of work that requires training and a formal qualification.
examples: Teaching is a demanding *profession*.
He left the legal *profession* at forty.
Nursing and law are very different *professions*.

gloss: A fixed amount of money paid to an employee, usually monthly or yearly.
examples: The *salary* is a little lower than I hoped.
She's on a *salary*, so she doesn't get overtime.
*Salaries* here haven't gone up in three years.

gloss: An increase in the money you are paid.
examples: I asked my boss for a *raise*.
He got a five percent *raise* in January.
Nobody's gotten *raises* since the merger.
contrast: American; the British call it a pay rise.

gloss: A move to a more senior job in the same organization.
examples: She got a *promotion* after two years.
The *promotion* came with a bigger office.
They announced three *promotions* at once.

gloss: The act of formally quitting a job, or the letter announcing it.
examples: He handed in his *resignation* on Monday.
Her *resignation* took everyone by surprise.
Two *resignations* landed in the same week.
contrast: The g is pronounced here, though it is silent in *resign*.

gloss: The point when a person stops working for good, and the years after it.
examples: He's saving for *retirement*.
She took early *retirement* last spring.
There's a party for his *retirement* on Friday.

gloss: Regular money paid to someone after they stop working.
examples: He gets a small *pension* from the city.
The *pension* barely covers the rent.
Public workers still have decent *pensions*.

gloss: The health insurance, paid leave, and other extras an employer provides.
examples: The pay is average but the *benefits* are great.
Part-timers don't get *benefits*.
*Benefits* kick in after ninety days.
contrast: Plural in this sense — *a benefit* on its own just means an advantage.

gloss: Time off work for rest or travel.
examples: I'm taking a *vacation* in August.
She's on *vacation* until the tenth.
We get three weeks of *vacation* a year.
contrast: American; the British say holiday for the same thing.

gloss: Officially approved time away from work.
examples: She's on maternity *leave* until March.
He took two weeks of unpaid *leave*.
You have to request *leave* a month ahead.
contrast: Uncountable in this sense — never *leaves* for time off work.

gloss: Hours worked beyond the normal schedule, or the extra pay for them.
examples: He's been working a lot of *overtime*.
*Overtime* pays time and a half.
There's no *overtime* in the budget this month.

gloss: A set period of working hours, one of several covering the day.
examples: My *shift* starts at six in the morning.
She picked up an extra *shift* on Saturday.
The night *shifts* are hardest to fill.

gloss: The regular trip between home and work.
examples: My *commute* is about forty minutes each way.
He reads on the *commute* into the city.
Long *commutes* wear people down.

gloss: The person who directs and checks another employee's work.
examples: Ask your *supervisor* before you leave early.
My *supervisor* signed off on the request.
Both *supervisors* were in the meeting.

gloss: Someone you work with.
examples: A *coworker* gave me a ride home.
She's friendly with everyone, but her *coworkers* barely know her.
Two *coworkers* covered my shift.
contrast: Also written co-worker.

gloss: A senior manager who helps run a company.
examples: She's an *executive* at a media company.
The *executive* flew in for one meeting.
*Executives* got bonuses; nobody else did.

gloss: A student or trainee doing short-term work to gain experience.
examples: The *intern* handles the scheduling.
She started here as an *intern*.
We take on four *interns* every summer.
contrast: Stress moves: the noun is IN-turn, the verb *to intern* is in-TURN.

gloss: A person being considered for a job.
examples: He's the strongest *candidate* we've seen.
The *candidate* asked good questions.
They narrowed it down to three *candidates*.

gloss: A formal written request for a job or a place somewhere.
examples: I sent in my *application* last night.
The *application* takes about half an hour.
They got six hundred *applications* for one job.

gloss: A meeting where an employer questions someone applying for a job.
examples: I have an *interview* Thursday afternoon.
The *interview* lasted almost two hours.
She went through four *interviews* before the offer.

gloss: A formal proposal to hire someone at a stated salary.
examples: She got an *offer* from a firm in Boston.
The *offer* came in below what he wanted.
He turned down two *offers* last month.

gloss: Teaching that prepares someone to do a job.
examples: New hires get two weeks of *training*.
She's still in *training*.
The *training* was mostly videos.
contrast: Uncountable — say *a lot of training*, not *trainings*.

gloss: An organized group of workers formed to protect their rights.
examples: The *union* is negotiating a new contract.
He's been in the *union* since 1998.
Two *unions* represent workers at the plant.

gloss: A refusal to work, used to press an employer for something.
examples: The drivers went on *strike* for two weeks.
The *strike* ended with a wage increase.
There were *strikes* at three plants that summer.

gloss: The dismissal of workers because there is not enough work or money.
examples: He lost his job in the last *layoff*.
The *layoff* hit the whole department.
There were *layoffs* right before the holidays.

gloss: The amount of work a person is expected to do.
examples: My *workload* has doubled since she left.
They finally cut back his *workload*.
*Workloads* are uneven across the team.

gloss: Exhaustion caused by working too hard for too long.
examples: *Burnout* is why she quit.
There's a lot of *burnout* in that field.
He's showing every sign of *burnout*.

gloss: The general mood and confidence of a group of people.
examples: *Morale* is pretty low right now.
The bonuses did nothing for *morale*.
New management brought *morale* back up.
contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable, muh-RAL — not the same word as *moral*.

gloss: The people employed by an organization.
examples: All *personnel* have to badge in.
*Personnel* were evacuated within minutes.
Ask *personnel* about your benefits.
contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, pur-suh-NEL — don't confuse it with *personal*.

gloss: Someone employed to clean and maintain a building.
examples: The *janitor* let us into the room.
He worked as a *janitor* while going to school.
The *janitors* come through around eight.
contrast: American; the British say caretaker.

gloss: Someone who works for several clients instead of one employer.
examples: She's been a *freelancer* since 2019.
We brought in a *freelancer* to finish the design.
Most of our writers are *freelancers*.

gloss: A person or company hired to do a job without being an employee.
examples: He works there as a *contractor*, not staff.
The *contractor* bills by the hour.
Half the team are *contractors*.

gloss: A company that sells goods or services to another company.
examples: We switched *vendors* last year.
The *vendor* is late with the shipment.
Three *vendors* bid on the job.

gloss: An arrangement with a bank or company, or a client a company works for.
examples: She handles our biggest *account*.
The money went into the wrong *account*.
He lost two *accounts* in one quarter.

gloss: The money left over after costs are paid.
examples: The store finally turned a *profit*.
*Profits* were up eight percent.
They sold the building at a *profit*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *prophet*.

gloss: A planned piece of work with a goal and an end date.
examples: I'm on a new *project* starting Monday.
The *project* is running two weeks late.
She's juggling three *projects* at once.
contrast: Stress moves: the noun is PRAH-jekt, the verb *to project* is pruh-JEKT.

gloss: A single piece of work that has to be done.
examples: That's the first *task* on my list.
It's a boring *task*, but somebody has to do it.
He knocked out three *tasks* before lunch.

gloss: A job or duty given to someone.
examples: She got the overseas *assignment*.
This *assignment* should take a couple of days.
He turns down *assignments* he doesn't like.

gloss: Something you are required to do as part of a job.
examples: Answering the phone isn't part of my *duty*.
Her *duties* include scheduling and payroll.
He listed all the *duties* in the job posting.

gloss: A set of steps followed to get something done.
examples: The hiring *process* takes about a month.
We're changing the whole *process* next quarter.
Both *processes* end up in the same place.
contrast: Americans say PRAH-sess; the British say PROH-sess.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: How well someone does their work, or a single show put on for an audience.
examples: Her *performance* this year has been excellent.
We talk about *performance* in the annual review.
The company's *performance* slipped in the fall.

gloss: A formal statement that something is wrong or unfair.
examples: A customer filed a *complaint* about the delay.
The *complaint* went straight to HR.
They've had three *complaints* about the same guy.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A message sent electronically, or the system for sending such messages.
examples: I'll send you an *email* this afternoon.
Just let me know by *email*.
There were ninety unread *emails* after vacation.

gloss: The place where incoming email messages arrive.
examples: My *inbox* is out of control.
It's sitting in your *inbox* somewhere.
She keeps two separate *inboxes*.

gloss: A file sent along with an email.
examples: You forgot the *attachment* again.
The *attachment* is too big to send.
Don't open *attachments* from people you don't know.

gloss: The people who run a company, or the work of running it.
examples: *Management* decided to close the store.
She moved into *management* last year.
There's no trust between staff and *management*.

gloss: The work of promoting and selling a company's products.
examples: She works in *marketing*.
They spent a fortune on *marketing*.
The whole *marketing* team is remote.

gloss: The part of a business that sells, or the amount of goods sold.
examples: *Sales* were down last quarter.
He's been in *sales* his whole career.
The *sales* team hit its target.
contrast: Plural in this sense, with a plural verb: *sales are up*.

gloss: People working together effectively toward a shared goal.
examples: That project took real *teamwork*.
There's not much *teamwork* on that floor.
The whole training is about *teamwork*.

gloss: Deep knowledge or skill in a particular area.
examples: We hired her for her *expertise* in tax law.
That's outside my *expertise*.
The team lacks *expertise* in this area.
contrast: Uncountable — never *expertises*.
